subject: Observability benchmark
summary:
**What slowed down:** The checkout flow (POST /api/orders, GET /api/cart) became extremely slow, with order-service p95 latency spiking from ~48ms baseline to 10 seconds during the worst period (05:03–05:45 UTC, Oct 29).

**Why — the main bottleneck was order-service's database layer.** Slow queries on the sessions, orders, and products tables (613ms–2575ms) appeared intermittently from Oct 28 17:12 UTC onward, progressively worsening. By 04:52–04:56 UTC Oct 29, queries hit 1–2.5 seconds. This likely saturated the database connection pool, causing the order-service to spend 11–14 seconds per request waiting for connections — confirmed by "database connection timeout" errors appearing from 08:16 UTC onward. Traces show the time was entirely inside order-service with downstream calls completing in milliseconds (e.g., user-service call took just 25ms).

**Contributing factor — user-service degradation:** A separate issue at 02:08–02:44 UTC Oct 29 caused user-service p95 to hit 10s. The auth-cache-refresh job fell behind (530s lag, 834 stale keys), memory hit 95%, and this independently slowed checkout flows calling user-service.

**Representative trace:** `4715b7764646608b1a48f1b3a2cec04b` — POST /api/orders taking 17.6s total, with 12.7s spent inside order-service (no child spans = time in DB operations), user-service call only 25ms.

**What backs this conclusion:** Prometheus p95 metrics (run 12), slow DB query warnings across sessions/orders/products tables (run 27), database connection timeout errors (run 28), trace span timing confirming bottleneck inside order-service (runs 17, 23), and slow request logs showing 3.4–14.8s POST /api/orders durations (run 25).

impact.summary: Checkout p95 latency degraded from ~48ms to 10s during the worst spike (05:03–05:45 UTC Oct 29), with individual POST /api/orders requests taking 3.4–14.8 seconds. Error rates increased with 500/502/503 responses throughout. A separate user-service spike (02:08–02:44 UTC) also impacted checkout flows. Payment-service was largely unaffected.

findings.statement: The order-service database layer is the primary bottleneck causing checkout slowness. Slow queries on the sessions, orders, and products tables (613ms–2575ms) began appearing intermittently from Oct 28 17:12 UTC and escalated into connection pool saturation, with 'database connection timeout' errors appearing from 08:16 UTC onward on Oct 29. The worst spike was 05:03–05:45 UTC Oct 29 when order-service p95 latency hit 10s (baseline ~48ms).
findings.mechanism: Database layer degradation in order-service — slow queries on sessions/orders/products tables (613ms–2575ms) escalated to connection pool saturation, causing the service to spend 11–14 seconds per request waiting for database connections. The trace evidence confirms the time was spent entirely inside order-service with negligible downstream call latency (25ms to user-service).

findings.statement: User-service experienced a separate but concurrent degradation: its auth-cache-refresh job fell behind (lag up to 530 seconds, 834 stale keys), memory hit 95%, and p95 latency spiked to 8–10s from 02:08–02:44 UTC on Oct 29. This independently impacted checkout flows that call user-service for authentication.
findings.mechanism: The auth-cache-refresh background job fell behind by hundreds of seconds, accumulating stale cache keys and consuming 95% of memory, which degraded the user-service's ability to serve requests quickly.

findings.statement: Payment-service remained relatively stable with only occasional p95 spikes (up to 4.5s), while order-service and user-service experienced severe sustained p95 spikes reaching the histogram ceiling (10s).
findings.mechanism: Prometheus histogram_quantile measurements across three services over the full investigation window

findings.statement: Order-service error logs show a cascade of failures during the spike: 500/502/503 errors with messages including 'database connection timeout', 'internal server error', 'upstream service error', and 'request failed'. Retry attempts and high memory warnings (76%) also appeared.
findings.mechanism: Order-service logged increasing numbers of 500/502/503 errors during the spike period, including 'database connection timeout', 'internal server error', 'upstream service error', and 'request failed' messages. It also logged 'retry attempt 3 for upstream call' and 'high memory usage: 76%'.

findings.statement: Representative trace 4715b7764646608b1a48f1b3a2cec04b (POST /api/orders) shows the full 17.6s request breakdown: webapp 17.6s → api-gateway 15.9s → order-service 12.7s (no child spans — time spent in uninstrumented DB operations). Trace 68d875d7b3fd0552b7542f74963ec4b6 (GET /api/cart, 15.3s) confirms the same: order-service 11s with user-service call only 25ms.
findings.mechanism: Traces 4715b776 and 68d875d7 show that within order-service, downstream calls to user-service and payment-service completed in 25ms or less, while the order-service span itself took 11–13 seconds. No child spans exist for the database operations, meaning the time is spent in uninstrumented DB calls.

hypotheses.statement: Order-service database connection pool exhaustion is the root cause of the checkout slowness, triggered by progressively worsening slow queries on sessions/orders/products tables that saturated available connections.
hypotheses.test: Check database connection pool metrics (active/idle connections, wait time) for order-service during the spike period; if available, verify pool was at capacity.

hypotheses.statement: User-service cache refresh lag caused memory pressure (95%) which in turn caused request queuing and the user-service p95 spike at 02:08-02:44 UTC.
hypotheses.test: Check user-service memory metrics and request queue depth during the 02:00-03:00 UTC window to confirm memory pressure caused request queuing.

actions.title: Investigate order-service database connection pool and query performance
actions.rationale: The order-service database layer is the primary bottleneck: slow queries on sessions/orders/products tables and connection timeouts are causing checkout latency to spike to 10+ seconds.
actions.verification: Check DB connection pool utilization, active connections, and slow query log for sessions/orders/products tables during peak hours.

actions.title: Add missing indexes on sessions, orders, and products tables
actions.rationale: Slow database query warnings on these tables (1-2.5s) appeared intermittently for hours before the major spike, suggesting missing or degraded indexes.
actions.verification: Review EXPLAIN plans for the most frequent queries on sessions, orders, and products tables; add indexes if full table scans are found.

actions.title: Investigate and fix user-service auth-cache-refresh lag
actions.rationale: User-service experienced severe auth-cache-refresh lag (up to 530s, 834 stale keys) and 95% memory, causing its own p95 spike to 10s. This independently slows checkout flows that call user-service.
actions.verification: Check cache refresh job health, memory allocation, and whether the lag correlates with the p95 spikes at 02:08-02:44 UTC.

actions.title: Set up alerts on order-service database connection pool saturation and slow queries
actions.rationale: The slow database queries appeared for hours before the major latency spike. Early alerting on pool saturation or slow queries would allow intervention before customers notice.
actions.verification: Configure alerts on connection pool wait time > 500ms or slow query count > 5 per minute on order-service.

limitations.statement: No direct database connection pool metrics were available in Prometheus; the pool exhaustion conclusion is inferred from slow query warnings, connection timeout errors, and trace span timing rather than direct pool utilization measurements.

Database operations within order-service are not instrumented as spans, so we cannot pinpoint the exact query or connection wait that consumed the 11–13s per request; we can only infer it from the absence of child spans and the slow query/error log messages.
The Tempo trace search returned incomplete results (hit the 20-trace limit), so we may not have seen the very worst or earliest affected traces.
